description: We are a team of Industrial Engineering students. We are interested in optimization, data analysis, modeling, and project management.
summary:
Earth Data Detective is a bilingual (English/Turkish) web tool that transforms students and curious members of the public into data detectives. The user can select a location on an interactive map or begin with one of four guided demo cases, such as the shrinking Aral Sea or Lake Tuz. They then select from ten Earth-science variables, each of which has a plain-language definition: temperature, precipitation, soil moisture, evaporation, water vapor, sea ice, ocean surface temperature, albedo and solar radiation. The tool retrieves MERRA-2 and CERES/SRB products from the NASA POWER API in real monthly cadence from 1981 to the present. The app removes the seasonal cycle for each series and plots the time series. It gives the rate of change per year and per decade and tests for significance using a Mann-Kendall test, a Theil–Sen slope and a 95% confidence interval. These are corrected for autocorrelation, so that slow natural wiggles are not confused with trends. Users can compare several regions, see real-data world maps for early vs recent periods, and know when a trend is not yet statistically significant.

It’s important because it tells us not only what’s changing and where, but how confidently we can be honest.
details:
What it does

Earth Data Detective lets anyone check whether part of our planet is really changing. You click a place on the map, or start with one of our guided cases: the shrinking Aral Sea, Lake Tuz, the water cycle or the Arctic. Then you pick up to four of ten NASA variables, such as temperature, rainfall, soil moisture or sea ice. Each one comes with a short, plain explanation.

The app pulls real monthly data from the NASA POWER API, from 1981 to today, and draws the time series. Then it answers the questions that matter: How fast is it changing? Is the change real, or could it just be noise? Where else is it happening? World maps compare the early 1980s with the 2020s, so you can see a trend rising in one region and falling in another.

Why it matters

We built it for students and curious people who want to work like real data detectives. Seeing a line go up is easy. Knowing whether that rise means anything is harder, and we wanted the app to teach exactly that. When a trend isn’t significant yet, the app says so and explains why, instead of hiding it.

How we built it

We wrote it in Python with Streamlit. pandas, NumPy, SciPy and statsmodels do the analysis, Plotly draws the charts and maps, and Folium handles the interactive map. All data comes from NASA POWER. 122 automated tests check the numbers against the API and keep the statistics honest. A normal laptop was all the hardware we needed.

What we cared about

Honesty came first. We use only real data, with no filled gaps or invented values. We remove the seasonal cycle and correct for natural slow wiggles so they don’t fake a trend, and we tell users plainly where our limits are. We also kept it simple enough for a high-school student, and made it work in both English and Turkish.
